name: RDFLib
purpose: Python library for working with RDF: parsers and serialisers for many formats, an in-memory and pluggable store, SPARQL 1.1 query and update support, and graph manipulation.
journalism_use_case: Working with linked-data sources an investigation actually encounters: querying Wikidata via SPARQL for structured facts about companies and officials, consuming government linked-data releases, or building a small RDF graph that connects entities across datasets with explicit, inspectable relationships.
pros: SPARQL support means you can query Wikidata directly for structured entity data — company registrations, officeholders, ownership statements — which is a substantial free data source for investigations
Explicit triple-based relationships make a knowledge graph auditable: every edge has a stated provenance and type, unlike an inferred embedding-based relation
BSD-3-Clause with long-term active maintenance (7.6.0 released 2026-02-13; pushed 2026-11-17) and a stable community (2,563 stars)
Format breadth means you can consume whatever serialisation a government or academic source publishes
cons: RDF has a steep conceptual overhead for the payoff in most newsroom work: for connecting entities across two datasets, a relational table or a property graph is usually simpler and clearer
In-memory store limits graph size, and scaling means a triple store (Oxigraph, Jena) which is another service to run
SPARQL is unfamiliar to most data journalists, so the practical barrier is skills rather than software
Release cadence is slow (February 2026 release against November commits), consistent with a mature library but awkward for pinning
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 2,563 stars with release 7.6.0 (2026-02-13), pushed 2026-11-17, BSD-3-Clause. RDFLib is the standard Python RDF library, which is well established in the linked-data ecosystem.
assessment: Integrate it specifically for Wikidata and linked-data access rather than as a knowledge-graph strategy — querying Wikidata for structured entity facts is the concrete, high-value use and it does not require adopting RDF for your own data. For your profile I would keep investigation graphs in FollowTheMoney or a property graph where the vocabulary fits investigative practice, and use RDFLib as the bridge to external structured sources.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 7.6.0 (2026-02-13), 2,563 stars, BSD-3-Clause. Same-day commits on a mature library with a slow deliberate release cadence — stability rather than stagnation.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Wikidata content is CC0; other linked-data sources vary.
licence_restrictions: None material for the library. Note that Wikidata's CC0 licensing makes it unusually safe to build on, which is part of its value.
costs: No fee, negligible resources for modest graphs. A triple store for larger graphs is additional infrastructure. Estimate.
privacy: Local library. SPARQL queries to Wikidata or another endpoint disclose your queries to that endpoint — relevant if the entities you are researching are sensitive, in which case a local Wikidata mirror is the alternative.
alternatives: Direct SPARQL HTTP queries to Wikidata without the library, for simple lookups
FollowTheMoney plus nomenklatura for investigative entity modelling
Oxigraph as a lightweight triple store when the graph outgrows memory

name: Oxigraph
purpose: RDF triple store written in Rust with SPARQL 1.1 query and update support, available as an embeddable library, a Python binding and a standalone HTTP server.
journalism_use_case: A local SPARQL endpoint for investigation data: load a Wikidata subset plus your own entity statements into one store and query across them, so a question like 'which companies in my leak have a Wikidata-recorded director who also holds public office' becomes a single query.
pros: Embeddable and lightweight, so a local triple store is a file and a process rather than a Java service — a materially lower operational bar than Jena or Blazegraph
SPARQL 1.1 including update means you can combine external linked data with your own assertions in one queryable graph, which is the useful pattern
Apache-2.0 with steady active maintenance (v0.5.13, 2026-10-22; pushed 2026-11-15) and a clean, focused codebase (2,050 stars)
Rust implementation gives predictable performance and memory behaviour at the scale a newsroom graph reaches
cons: RDF and SPARQL skills remain the barrier, and the tool does nothing to lower it — the conceptual cost is the same as with RDFLib
Smaller community than the established Java triple stores, so there is less guidance for unusual queries or performance tuning
Scales well for newsroom-sized graphs but is not a competitor to large-scale distributed triple stores if your graph becomes very large
Effectively a single-maintainer project, which for a store holding investigation data is a continuity consideration
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 2,050 stars with release v0.5.13 (2026-10-22), pushed 2026-11-15, Apache-2.0. Oxigraph is known in the RDF community as the lightweight modern alternative to Java triple stores.
assessment: The right triple store if you decide RDF is the correct model for an investigation graph — and the embeddability is what makes that decision affordable. For your profile I would reach for it in one specific scenario: when you want to combine a Wikidata subset with your own entity assertions and query across both, which is genuinely powerful and hard to do otherwise. For most entity work, FollowTheMoney plus a relational store remains simpler.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release v0.5.13 (2026-10-22), 2,050 stars, Apache-2.0. Regular releases with current commits from a focused maintainer.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Loaded data carries its own licence — Wikidata is CC0, other sources vary.
costs: No fee. Disk and memory proportional to graph size; a Wikidata subset plus investigation data fits comfortably on one machine. Estimate.
privacy: Fully local, so queries over sensitive investigation data disclose nothing — the key advantage over querying a public SPARQL endpoint with your entity names.
alternatives: RDFLib's in-memory store for small graphs
Apache Jena or Blazegraph for larger, more established triple stores
Neo4j Community or DuckDB for property-graph and relational approaches that most teams find easier

name: Kùzu
purpose: Embeddable property-graph database with Cypher query support, columnar storage and vectorised execution, designed as the graph equivalent of DuckDB.
journalism_use_case: Would have been the natural choice for an investigation graph: an embedded property-graph database with Cypher, so entity-relationship analysis over a leak could run in-process with no server — the pattern DuckDB established for tabular analysis.
pros: The embedded property-graph model is exactly right for investigative graph analysis: Cypher queries over entities and relationships with no server to operate
Columnar vectorised execution gave genuinely good performance on analytical graph queries, better than embedded alternatives
MIT licensed with a clean design and good documentation at the point development stopped
cons: ARCHIVED: the GitHub API reports archived=true with the final release v0.11.3 on 2025-10-10 and the last push the same day — read-only, with 4,022 stars at archival. This is a significant loss in a category with few good options
A graph database holding your investigation data is the worst category of dependency to have frozen: migration means re-modelling, not just re-importing
Commercial company behind it, and the archival suggests the business did not sustain the open project — a pattern worth noting when evaluating other open-core graph tools
No successor named in the repository, so the migration path is yours to choose
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The decisive documented fact, established in this session: archived=true per the GitHub API on 2026-11-17, final release v0.11.3 (2025-10-10), 4,022 stars — recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md L10. This is a recent archival of a tool that was gaining adoption, and it has not propagated into most recommendation lists.
assessment: Avoid for new deployment, and know the archival if you see Kùzu recommended — it was a genuinely good answer to embedded graph analysis and is now frozen. For your profile the practical alternatives are Neo4j Community (a server, GPL-3.0) for property-graph work, DuckDB with recursive SQL for many graph-shaped questions, or NetworkX for in-memory analysis. The broader lesson for your planning: open-core commercial infrastructure can be withdrawn, and a graph database is an expensive thing to migrate away from.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2025-10-10, latest release v0.11.3 published the same day, 4,022 stars, MIT licence. Archived by the maintainer with a final release — unambiguous and recent.
licence_restrictions: None, and the MIT licence means a fork is legally straightforward — though maintaining a database engine is not.
costs: No fee. Not worth adopting; any use means accepting fork-and-maintain responsibility for a database engine.
privacy: Embedded and local, which was part of its appeal.
alternatives: Neo4j Community Edition for property-graph work with Cypher, accepting a server and GPL-3.0
DuckDB with recursive SQL for many relationship queries without a graph database
NetworkX or igraph for in-memory graph analysis
blockers: Archived as of 2025-10-10 — a frozen database engine is an unacceptable dependency for investigation data

name: MLflow
purpose: Platform for machine-learning lifecycle management: experiment tracking, parameter and metric logging, artefact storage, model registry and, in recent versions, LLM tracing and evaluation.
journalism_use_case: Provenance for AI-assisted analysis: when a model classified ten thousand documents and three of those classifications informed a story, MLflow records which model version, parameters and prompt produced them — so an editor's question about how a finding was produced has a recorded answer rather than a recollection.
pros: Experiment tracking turns AI-assisted analysis from an undocumented process into a recorded one, which is a genuine editorial requirement that almost no newsroom currently meets
Model registry and artefact storage mean the exact model and parameters behind a published finding can be retrieved months later — the practical definition of reproducibility
Apache-2.0 under Linux Foundation governance with very active development (v3.18.0, 2026-11-04; pushed 2026-11-17) and strong adoption (28,853 stars)
LLM tracing support in recent versions extends the same provenance model to prompt-based work, which is where newsroom AI actually sits
cons: Designed for machine-learning teams, so the conceptual model (experiments, runs, registered models) takes translation to fit newsroom analysis workflows
Operating a tracking server plus artefact storage is real infrastructure for a benefit that is organisational rather than immediately visible — it will be skipped unless someone insists
Databricks' commercial interest shapes direction, and the managed offering is the vendor's product
For simple prompt-based work, simonw/llm's SQLite logging gives most of the provenance benefit at a fraction of the effort
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 28,853 stars with release v3.18.0 (2026-11-04), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0 under Linux Foundation governance. Adoption in ML engineering is well established; journalism use is unestablished here.
assessment: Worth adopting if you run model-based analysis at any scale, chiefly as an accountability measure rather than a productivity one — the value appears when a published finding is challenged. For your profile, start with the lighter option: simonw/llm's automatic SQLite logging covers prompt-based work with no infrastructure, and MLflow becomes worthwhile when you are training or fine-tuning models, or running classification at a scale where version drift is a real risk.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v3.18.0 (2026-11-04), 28,853 stars, Apache-2.0. Same-day commits and frequent releases under foundation governance with substantial corporate contribution.
licence_restrictions: None material. Databricks' managed MLflow is a separate commercial service.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: a tracking server, a database and artefact storage — one VM plus object storage for a newsroom. Managed offerings priced separately (not verified). Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted keeps experiment data and artefacts internal. Note that logged artefacts may include document content, so the tracking store inherits the sensitivity of what you process.
alternatives: simonw/llm's SQLite prompt logging for lightweight provenance on prompt-based work — recommended starting point
DVC for data and pipeline versioning rather than experiment tracking
A disciplined notebook plus version control, which is cruder but genuinely used

name: Sigstore Cosign
purpose: Tool for signing, verifying and storing signatures for container images and other software artefacts, with keyless signing via OIDC identity and transparency-log recording.
journalism_use_case: Verifying what you deploy and attesting what you publish: signature verification on the container images running your SecureDrop, archive or analysis infrastructure, and signed attestations for datasets you release so downstream users can confirm they came from you unmodified.
pros: Addresses a real and ignored risk: a newsroom running unverified container images in its source-protection path is trusting whatever a registry served, and signature verification closes that
Keyless signing via OIDC removes the key-management burden that otherwise prevents signing from happening at all — the practical reason most organisations do not sign anything
Transparency-log recording means signatures are publicly auditable, so a tampered artefact is detectable rather than merely unsigned
Apache-2.0 under OpenSSF governance with very active maintenance (v3.1.4, 2026-10-20; pushed 2026-11-16) and strong adoption (6,444 stars)
cons: Keyless signing records an identity in a public transparency log, which for a newsroom signing artefacts means publishing an organisational identity — usually fine, occasionally a consideration
Verification only helps if you actually enforce it in deployment, and adding policy enforcement to a deployment pipeline is the work most teams skip after installing the tool
Container-and-artefact oriented, so it addresses software supply chain rather than document or media provenance (C2PA covers that)
Concepts (attestations, transparency logs, OIDC identities) take orientation for a team without supply-chain security background
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 6,444 stars with release v3.1.4 (2026-10-20), pushed 2026-11-16, Apache-2.0 under OpenSSF governance. Sigstore's adoption across major open-source ecosystems is well documented and is why signature verification is now practical.
assessment: Worth integrating into deployment for the specific infrastructure that protects sources — if you run SecureDrop, an archive or a document pipeline from container images, verifying signatures is a cheap, meaningful hardening step. For your profile the second use is also worth considering: signing datasets and document releases so partners and readers can verify they came from you unaltered, which pairs with C2PA for media and matters when your work is republished or misattributed.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v3.1.4 (2026-10-20), 6,444 stars, Apache-2.0. Regular releases under OpenSSF governance with broad industry participation.
costs: No fee. The public Sigstore infrastructure is free to use. Cost is engineering time to add verification to deployment. Estimate.
privacy: Keyless signing records your signing identity in a public transparency log, which is a deliberate disclosure. Verification itself contacts the transparency log, revealing what you are verifying — minor, but worth knowing for an air-gapped deployment, where offline verification with keys is the alternative.
alternatives: Traditional GPG signing with your own keys, avoiding the transparency-log disclosure at the cost of key management
C2PA for media and document provenance rather than software artefacts
Pinning image digests, which gives immutability without authenticity
